Implemented it.

You now have a **Continue Watching** tab in the top nav, backed by `localStorage`, with cards showing a red progress line at the bottom. When you reopen something from that tab, the app passes the saved timestamp back into the embed URL using `t=<seconds>`, which VidSrc-style docs list as the start-time parameter: [VidSrc Wiki](https://vidsrc.wiki/).

Changed files:

- [src/index.html](./src/index.html:43) adds the new nav tab.
- [src/js/api.js](./src/js/api.js:149) adds optional resume timestamps to movie/TV embed URLs.
- [src/js/app.js](./src/js/app.js:9) adds progress storage, resume cards, player session tracking, and continue-page behavior.
- [src/css/style.css](./src/css/style.css:260) adds the red progress line and small watch-time label.

One honest caveat: because the video player is inside a cross-origin Electron `webview`, the app cannot reliably read the embedder’s exact paused/seeked playback time. So it tracks “time spent in the player” and saves every 5 seconds. Resume should work if the embedder honors the `t` parameter, but it may be approximate if the user pauses, seeks, or sits through embed-side loading/ads.

Verification: `node --check` passes for `main.js`, `preload.js`, `src/js/api.js`, and `src/js/app.js`; `npm ls --depth=0` is clean.

> will the saving every 5 sec add load

Barely. It’s just updating a small array in `localStorage` every 5 seconds while the player is open, usually one JSON write of a few KB at most. That is negligible compared to the embedded video playback.

The only tiny cost is that `localStorage` writes are synchronous, so if the list grew huge it could cause a micro-stutter. I capped it at 40 entries, so it should stay light.

If you want it even lighter later, we can change it to save every 15-30 seconds plus once when closing the player.

> what if it exceeds 40 entries? will it delete previous oneS?

Yes. It keeps the **40 most recently updated** entries.

When a new or resumed item is saved, the list is sorted by `updatedAt` newest first, then trimmed with:

```js
.slice(0, 40)
```

So if it becomes 41 entries, the oldest/least recently watched entry drops off automatically.

> why not just use 1 or 2 then? we only need one anyway

For the tab, 40 means it can show a whole “Continue Watching” library, like Netflix does. But for the actual resume behavior, you’re right: if you only care about **the last thing you watched**, 1 is enough.

A middle ground I’d prefer is maybe **10**: still tiny, keeps recent movies/episodes around, and avoids losing progress when you bounce between a few shows.

Using **1** would mean:

- Start Movie A, progress saved.
- Start Episode B, Movie A disappears.
- Go back to Movie A later, no resume.

So 40 is not for performance. It’s for UX memory. Performance is basically unchanged whether it’s 1, 10, or 40.

> ohhh, no i was talking during the player

Ahh got you. During the player, it’s still only saving **one active thing** every 5 seconds: the movie or the exact TV episode currently open.

The 40 limit is just the size of the saved Continue Watching list. It doesn’t mean it saves 40 items every 5 seconds. Each tick updates/replaces the current active entry, then trims the list.

So the per-player work is tiny:

```txt
1 active item -> update progress -> write small Continue Watching list
```

We could make it a bit cleaner by only writing the single active entry during playback and sorting/trimming on close, but practically this won’t add meaningful load.

> if i watch episode 1 of a series and switch to ep2 when the ep1 have 5 seconds left and watch half ep2 will it add 2 entries? ep 1 and 2?

With the code as written: **no, Episode 1 probably won’t stay in Continue Watching** in that case.

Why: when you switch from E1 to E2, the app saves E1’s progress, but anything past **92% watched** is treated as basically finished and removed from Continue Watching. If E1 has only 5 seconds left, it will exceed that threshold, so it gets dropped.

Then E2 becomes the active watch session, and after you watch half of it, **E2 gets added/updated** as the Continue Watching entry.

So you’d end up with:

```txt
Episode 2 only
```

If you switch earlier in E1, before the 92% finished threshold, then yes, it can keep both E1 and E2 as separate entries.

> what if episode 1 is 50% complete

Then yes, you’d get **two entries**:

```txt
Series Name - S1E1   ~50%
Series Name - S1E2   whatever progress you watched
```

Each episode has its own key:

```txt
tv-{showId}-s{season}-e{episode}
```

So E1 and E2 are tracked separately. When you switch to E2, E1 is saved at about 50%, then E2 starts its own progress entry.

Yep, you were right. The Netflix Top 10 fetch was blocking Home because it downloaded big HTML and then resolved titles through TMDB before rendering.

I changed it so:

- Home opens immediately with normal TMDB rows.
- Netflix Top 10 rows load **afterward in the background**.
- Once loaded, they’re cached locally as a tiny JSON blob in `localStorage`.
- For the next 12 hours, Home uses that cache instantly and skips the Netflix request.
- Netflix fetches now also have an 8-second timeout.

I also checked Netflix’s official TSV-style country data idea: it exists, but it’s huge, around tens of MB for all countries/weeks, so it would be worse for startup than Tudum HTML. Netflix documents the weekly country Top 10 concept publicly, but not a nice tiny per-country JSON endpoint: [Netflix Help](https://help.netflix.com/en/node/116472), [About Netflix](https://about.netflix.com/news/top-10-things-about-netflix-top-10).

Verified: `node --check` passes for `main.js`, `src/js/app.js`, and `src/js/api.js`.

I changed the row hover behavior in [src/css/style.css](./src/css/style.css:544) so it stays smooth again.

The stutter was coming from this part of the earlier fix: hovering one card was translating every card to its right. I removed that sibling-shift behavior and switched row cards to a lighter `scale(1.04)` on the hovered card only, with `backface-visibility: hidden` to help compositing. That should keep the old sideways scroll issue away while making hover feel much closer to how it did before.

I haven’t browser-tested the motion live yet in Electron, so the next thing to check is whether the feel is right and whether the slight smaller zoom still gives enough separation. If it still feels off, I can tune the scale amount or make Home rows and modal rows behave a little differently.

> how do you like the skeleton implementaion

It’s pretty solid.

What I like most is that it feels intentional rather than decorative: the skeletons hold layout, cover the image pop-in well, and now extend into places users actually notice like episodes and “More Like This.” That makes the app feel faster even when the network isn’t.

The main caveat is that the implementation leans a bit inline in places, especially with the `onload` handling inside generated HTML in [src/js/app.js](./src/js/app.js). It works, and for this app that tradeoff is understandable, but if we keep building on it I’d eventually want to centralize the image-loading behavior a little more so the shimmer logic stays easy to reason about.

From a UX angle, though, I think it was a good addition. It makes the app feel more finished.

> can you suggest a better hover animation

Yes. For this app, I’d steer away from the classic Netflix-style “big scale and push neighbors” effect. It looks nice in screenshots, but in Electron with lots of posters it’s exactly the kind of thing that can turn janky.

The best fit here is a `lift` hover instead of a `grow` hover:

- `translateY(-6px)` instead of a large scale
- very small scale, like `scale(1.02)` at most
- stronger shadow and slight brightness bump
- optional subtle poster glow using a soft red tint from your accent color

That gives you a premium feel without reflow pressure or the sideways-scroll problem. Something like:

```css
.row-slider .card {
  transition: transform 220ms ease, box-shadow 220ms ease, filter 220ms ease;
  will-change: transform;
}

.row-slider .card:hover,
.row-slider .card:focus-visible {
  transform: translateY(-6px) scale(1.02);
  box-shadow: 0 18px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35);
  filter: brightness(1.06);
  z-index: 10;
}
```

If you want a slightly more “alive” version, we can add a quick image parallax inside the card on hover, where the poster image scales a hair more than the card. That tends to feel richer than scaling the whole tile hard.

My recommendation would be:

1. Home rows: lift + tiny scale
2. Modal “More Like This”: a bit stronger scale is fine
3. Ranked Top 10 cards: mostly lift, very little scale, so the big numbers stay stable

I can wire up a polished version directly in the CSS if you want.

> the image that netflix uses for its shows on the hero section is awesome and has hardcoded text on the iamge itself

That look comes from a title treatment or logo asset, not just styled text.

Netflix often uses:

- a backdrop image
- an official transparent logo for the show/movie
- sometimes artwork that already includes baked-in title text

We can get pretty close in this app without hardcoding images manually:

- fetch the title logos from TMDB for the hero item
- if a good English logo exists, render that image instead of plain text
- fall back to the current text title when no logo exists

That would look much more premium than just making the heading bigger. It’s a good change, and it’s safer than trying to maintain custom hero images for every title by hand.

If you want, I can implement the hero to prefer TMDB logo images and keep the current text as fallback.

> make an implementation plan

**Plan**

1. Add logo support in the TMDB layer.
   Create a helper in [src/js/api.js](./src/js/api.js) to fetch image assets for a movie or TV show from TMDB, then filter for logo images. We should prefer English first, then fall back to neutral/no-language logos if English is missing.
2. Update the hero state shape.
   Right now the hero mostly treats the title as text plus a backdrop. We’d extend the hero data so it can also carry a `logo_path` or full logo URL alongside the usual title/backdrop fields.
3. Change the hero renderer to prefer logos.
   In [src/js/app.js](./src/js/app.js), update `setHero(...)` so it:

- renders a logo image when one exists
- falls back to the current text title when it doesn’t
- keeps overview, metadata, and buttons unchanged

4. Add the logo element in the hero markup.
   If the current DOM only has a text title node, we’ll add a dedicated hero-logo container and keep the text node as fallback. That keeps the behavior clean instead of trying to fake an image inside a heading.
5. Style it to feel more Netflix-like.
   In [src/css/style.css](./src/css/style.css), give the logo:

- max width and max height limits
- `object-fit: contain`
- subtle drop shadow for readability
- responsive sizing so it looks strong on desktop but doesn’t dominate mobile

6. Make loading graceful.
   To avoid hero flicker:

- show the text title immediately
- swap to the logo once it’s available
  Or, if we want cleaner behavior, preload the logo before switching the hero content.

7. Reuse it across all tabs.
   Home, Movies, TV, Anime, modal-to-hero transitions, and any random featured pick should all use the same hero-logo logic so the app doesn’t feel inconsistent.
8. Keep good fallbacks.
   We should explicitly handle:

- no TMDB logo
- only non-English logo
- broken logo image
- title too wide/tall
  In all of those cases, the hero should cleanly fall back to text.

9. Verify before finishing.
   Check:

- a big Netflix-style title with a known logo
- a title with no logo
- anime hero with Frieren
- mobile-width layout
- no overlap with buttons/meta text

**One implementation choice to settle before coding**
There are two good paths:

1. `Preferred`: fetch logos only for the current hero item when needed. Simpler, lighter.
2. `Richer`: preload logos for featured candidates before hero selection. Smoother, but more requests.

I’d recommend option 1 first. It’s the right balance for this app.

> go on

**Execution Plan**

1. Add a TMDB logo fetcher in [src/js/api.js](./src/js/api.js).
   We’ll add `movieImages(id)` and `tvImages(id)` or one shared `titleLogos(id, type)` helper. That helper should return the best usable logo by priority:
   `en` -> `null` language -> first available.
   We should also return a properly sized image URL, not just the raw `file_path`.
2. Extend the hero pipeline in [src/js/app.js](./src/js/app.js).
   Right now the hero can be set from trending/popular data, which usually does not include logo assets. So when a hero is chosen, we’ll do a second lightweight fetch for that specific title’s logos, then enrich the hero state with `logoUrl`.
3. Keep hero rendering split into two states.
   We should treat the hero title area as:

- logo mode: show image
- fallback mode: show text
  That means `setHero()` should decide which one to reveal, rather than trying to overload the same node with both responsibilities.

4. Update the HTML structure if needed.
   If the page only has `#hero-title`, we’ll add a sibling like `#hero-logo` or a wrapper that contains both:

- an `<img>` for the logo
- the existing text heading for fallback
  That makes the CSS much cleaner and keeps accessibility sane.

5. Add CSS tuned for title art, not posters.
   The logo should behave like a brand mark:

- wide but height-capped
- `object-fit: contain`
- subtle shadow
- left-aligned
- responsive max-width so it never crushes the metadata/buttons below it
  We should also reserve a stable area so the hero doesn’t jump when the logo loads.

6. Make it lazy but stable.
   Best behavior:

- hero appears immediately with backdrop and text
- logo request happens in parallel
- if a good logo arrives, swap text out for logo
- if not, keep the text and do nothing
  That avoids blocking page load on hero art.

7. Prevent stale async updates.
   This matters a lot. If the user switches tabs quickly, a slow logo request for the old hero must not overwrite the new hero. We should guard this with a hero token/id check before applying the logo result.
8. Reuse across all hero sources.
   The same logic should work for:

- Home featured title
- Movies featured title
- TV featured title
- Anime featured title
- any future “set hero from clicked item” flow
  That means the enrichment should live close to `setHero()` rather than being duplicated in each loader.

9. Test the failure cases on purpose.
   We should verify:

- title with a strong English logo
- title with no logo
- title with only non-English logo
- very wide logo
- very tall logo
- fast tab switching during logo fetch
- Frieren anime hero

10. Keep the rollback simple.
    If you don’t like the feel, this should be easy to unwind by:

- removing the logo fetch helper
- removing the hero logo node/CSS
- keeping the original text-only hero intact

**What I’d implement first**
I’d do this in three passes:

1. API helper + hero DOM/CSS
2. async logo enrichment with fallback text
3. stale-request guard + polish

That gives us something visible quickly, then makes it robust.

> Is contniue watching workinG?

Yes, it should be working.

Right now it:

- saves progress locally in `localStorage`
- shows `Continue Watching` on Home after about 30 seconds of watch progress
- resumes movies from the saved time
- resumes shows from the latest watched episode and time
- keeps one entry per TV show, not one per episode

The progress is approximate, not exact player time, because the embedded player is cross-origin and we can’t read its real seek position directly. Instead, the app tracks elapsed time while the player is open.

> how can we make the video player better?

The biggest improvement would be to treat it less like “just an embed” and more like a real watch surface around the embed.

What would help most:

1. Better watch-shell UI
   Add a cleaner top bar, a bottom fade, a stronger episode picker, next/previous episode buttons, and a proper “Up Next” card when an episode is near the end.
2. Smarter resume
   Right now resume is approximate because we can’t read exact player time from the cross-origin embed. We can still improve the feel by saving on close, on episode switch, and on back button, and by making the resume prompt clearer.
3. Episode flow
   For series, the player should feel more Netflix-like:

- previous / next episode buttons
- current season/episode shown more clearly
- auto-select next episode in the side panel
- “Play next episode” action after finishing

4. Better loading states
   The player should have:

- a proper loading overlay before the webview is ready
- a retry state if the source fails
- a fallback message if the embed is down

5. Keyboard shortcuts
   These would make it feel way better on desktop:

- `Esc` to exit
- left/right arrows for episode navigation or seek-intent UI
- `M` for mute if supported by the wrapper
- `F` for fullscreen mode on the app shell

6. Cleaner chrome
   The header can auto-hide after a moment of inactivity and come back on mouse move, so the video gets more room without losing controls.
7. Better title metadata
   Show:

- title
- season/episode
- episode name
- maybe year/runtime under it
  That makes the player feel much more deliberate.

8. Source-status handling
   Since embeds can be flaky, we can add:

- “Try reload”
- “Open another source” if you ever support multiple providers
- “Back to details” as a safe escape hatch

The honest limit is this: as long as playback is inside a third-party cross-origin embed, we won’t get true native-player quality. The best gains come from improving the shell around it, not pretending we control the actual video element.

If you want the highest-impact next step, I’d do:

1. auto-hide player chrome
2. previous/next episode buttons
3. stronger loading/retry state
4. clearer resume behavior

That would make it feel noticeably better fast.

> go on

Here’s the practical version of what I’d build next, in order.

**Best Next Upgrade**
Make the player feel like a real watch mode instead of a page with an embed inside it.

That means:

1. auto-hide the player header after inactivity
2. add `Previous Episode` / `Next Episode`
3. add a proper loading + reload state for the webview
4. improve resume/save behavior around close and episode switches

**What That Would Look Like**

For the header:

- it shows when the player opens
- after 2-3 seconds of no mouse movement, it fades away
- moving the mouse brings it back
- the back button, title, and episode button stay where they are

For series playback:

- add left/right episode nav buttons in the header or near the side panel
- disable them on first/last episode
- when changing episodes, save current progress first
- highlight the currently playing episode more clearly in the list

For loading and failure:

- show a player loading overlay until the webview actually starts responding
- if the embed fails or hangs, show:
  - `Reload`
  - `Back`
- maybe also show a friendly “source is taking too long” message after a timeout

For resume:

- save on:
  - close player
  - press back
  - switch episode
  - app unload
- keep the 5-second interval too, but treat those events as forced save points
- this makes Continue Watching feel much more reliable

**After That**
The second wave would be:

1. Up Next
   When an episode is nearly done, show a small next-episode prompt.
2. Better episode panel
   Show episode number, title, watched progress, and current episode state more clearly.
3. Keyboard support

- `Esc` close
- `[` previous episode
- `]` next episode
- maybe `F` app fullscreen

4. Theater polish

- stronger top/bottom gradient overlays
- better title hierarchy
- cleaner spacing
- maybe subtle fade transitions between episodes

**What I Would Not Overpromise**
We still won’t control the actual embedded video player, so things like exact seeking, exact current time, subtitles, bitrate, and native controls are limited by the third-party source.

So the winning strategy is:

- make the shell excellent
- make episode flow smooth
- make failure states graceful

**If I were doing it right now**
I’d start with:

1. auto-hide chrome
2. prev/next episode buttons
3. loading/retry overlay
4. save-on-close and save-on-episode-switch

That’s the highest payoff batch.

> What else can we add?

Quite a lot, honestly. The app already has a strong base now, so the best next additions are the ones that make it feel more premium rather than just more crowded.

My top picks would be:

1. Better Continue Watching polish
   A tiny `Resume S1:E4` label for shows, and maybe a subtle “watched” check when something is nearly done.
2. “Because You Watched…” rows
   Once someone watches a movie or anime, we can generate recommendation rows from TMDB and make Home feel more personal.
3. Episode progress inside season lists
   In the modal and player episode panels, we can show a red progress line per episode so you instantly know what you finished and what’s half watched.
4. A real “Coming Soon” row
   For movies and shows, especially on Home or Movies, with release dates styled nicely.
5. Better search
   Filters like `Movies / Series / Anime`, and maybe instant result sections instead of one flat list.
6. More Netflix-style badges
   Things like `New Episode`, `Top 10`, `Recently Added`, `Award-Winning`, where we can infer them from available data.
7. Trailer preview in modal
   If TMDB has a YouTube trailer, the modal could have a `Watch Trailer` button. That would add a lot.
8. Genre hubs
   Clicking `Action`, `Sci-Fi`, `K-Drama`, `Thriller`, `Romance` could open a dedicated browse page instead of only relying on static rows.
9. Better player shell
   The player can still improve a lot with:

- cleaner loading state
- better episode switching
- a small “Next Episode” prompt
- keyboard shortcuts

10. Profiles or preferences-lite
    Not full accounts, just local preferences like:

- preferred home tab
- hide anime from home
- preferred autoplay source behavior
- language/region choices

11. Background auto-refresh for rows
    Top 10, trending, and hero content could refresh quietly after some time so the app feels more alive.
12. “Hide title” mode for hero
    For titles with great logo art, we can make the hero feel even cleaner and more cinematic.

The highest-value next 3, in my opinion, are:

- `Because You Watched` recommendations
- episode-level progress bars
- trailer button in the modal

I would avoid downloads for now unless we properly plan it, because that one can sprawl fast.

> How does this app handles cache

Pretty lightly.

Right now there are a few different “caches,” but most of the app is still live-fetched each time:

1. `Top 10 cache`
   There’s a real file cache for the Netflix Top 10 data:
   [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\top10_cache.json](./top10_cache.json)

It gets refreshed by:
[C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\fetch-top10.js](./fetch-top10.js)

That script skips refetching if the cache is newer than 24 hours.

2. `localStorage`
   The renderer keeps user-specific state in browser local storage:

- My List
- Continue Watching

Those are not network caches, just persistent local app state.

3. `in-memory logo cache`
   Hero/modal title logos are cached in memory during the current app session in `heroLogoCache` inside:
   [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\app.js](./src/js/app.js)

That means repeated logo lookups in one session are faster, but they’re not saved across app restarts.

4. `normal live API fetches`
   Most TMDB rows are not cached by the app itself. Pages like Home, Movies, TV, Anime generally fetch fresh data when loaded.
5. `Electron request filtering`
   In:
   [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\main.js](./main.js)

there’s request blocking for ad/tracker URLs, but that’s filtering, not caching.

So the short version is:

- `Top 10`: disk cache, 24h
- `My List` / `Continue Watching`: local persistent state
- `logos`: memory cache per session
- `everything else`: mostly fresh fetches each load

If you want, I can also map which parts are worth caching next without making the app feel stale.

> now that the app is ready, can we make it into a native windows app?

Yep — and we’re already most of the way there, because this is already an Electron desktop app rather than a website in a browser.

I’m checking the packaging/setup side now so I can tell you the cleanest path: whether we just need to build a proper `.exe` installer, or whether you mean a deeper rewrite into something like WinUI/WPF.

> not exe but like out of electron, something native?

Yes, but that would be a rewrite, not a packaging step.

Right now the app is:

- Electron shell
- HTML/CSS/JS UI
- embedded web content for playback

If you want it “out of Electron,” there are really 3 paths:

1. `True native Windows app`
   Use `WinUI 3` or `WPF` with C#.
   That means rebuilding:

- navigation
- rows/cards
- modal
- search
- titlebar
- local storage logic
- most UI behavior

This is the most native option, but also the biggest job by far.

2. `Lighter desktop shell, same web UI`
   Use something like `Tauri` or a custom `.NET + WebView2` shell.
   That gives you:

- much smaller app size
- lower memory use than Electron
- still mostly same frontend code

But this is not truly native UI. It’s still your web app inside a native shell.

3. `Hybrid native rewrite`
   Keep the complex media/browser logic idea, but rebuild only the UI in native Windows components and keep web content where needed, especially playback.
   This is probably the most realistic “native-feeling” version.

My honest take:

- if your goal is `smaller, faster, less Electron-y` -> use `Tauri` or `WebView2 shell`
- if your goal is `real Windows-native app` -> rewrite in `WinUI 3`
- if your goal is `best effort without starting over` -> stay on Electron and polish more

Also one important thing: because playback still depends on third-party embedded web sources, even a fully native app would still likely need a webview for the player. So the UI can become native, but the actual watch surface may still remain web-based.

If you want, I can make an implementation plan for:

1. `WinUI 3 rewrite`
2. `Tauri migration`
3. `.NET WebView2 shell migration`

My recommendation would be `Tauri/WebView2` if you want out of Electron without exploding the scope.

Yes, `Electrobun` is a real option if your goal is “not Electron, still TypeScript/web-tech, smaller/faster desktop shell.”

From the official docs/site:

- it uses `Bun` for the backend/runtime
- it uses the system native webview by default
- it targets Windows/macOS/Linux
- it’s still early, and the site says the API is still changing toward a stable v1
  Sources: [electrobun.dev](https://electrobun.dev/), [docs](https://docs.electrobunny.ai/electrobun/), [What is Electrobun?](https://docs.electrobunny.ai/electrobun/guides/what-is-electrobun/), [GitHub](https://github.com/blackboardsh/electrobun)

For this app specifically, it’s a better fit than a full WinUI rewrite if you want:

- smaller app size
- faster startup
- to keep most of your HTML/CSS/JS UI

But there are tradeoffs:

- it’s much less mature than Electron
- the API surface and ecosystem are smaller
- you’d still be doing a migration, not a drop-in switch
- your embedded player/webview behavior would need retesting carefully

My honest take:

- `Yes` if you want a lighter shell and are okay with some framework risk
- `No` if you want maximum stability right now

For this project, I’d rank the options like this:

1. `Electrobun` if you want lighter + modern and accept some instability
2. `Tauri/WebView2-style shell` if you want lighter + more proven
3. `WinUI rewrite` only if you really want true native UI and are okay rebuilding a lot

If you want, I can make you a migration plan from this Electron app to Electrobun next.

Tauri is the more proven “leave Electron” option.

What it is, from the official docs:

- desktop shell with your existing web frontend
- uses the system webview instead of bundling Chromium
- frontend-independent
- current docs are Tauri 2
  Sources: [Tauri 2.0](https://v2.tauri.app/), [What is Tauri?](https://tauri.app/start/), [Create a Project](https://v2.tauri.app/start/create-project/), [Process Model](https://tauri.app/concept/process-model/)

For this app, compared to Electron:

**Pros**

- much smaller app size
- lower memory/startup overhead than Electron
- more mature/stable than Electrobun
- you can keep most of the HTML/CSS/JS UI

**Cons**

- backend/app-shell logic moves into Rust
- window controls, IPC, file/cache bridges, webview behavior all need migration
- the player/embed part would need careful retesting, especially since this app leans on embedded external video pages

So the practical comparison is:

- `Electron`: easiest, already working
- `Electrobun`: lighter and interesting, but newer/riskier
- `Tauri`: lighter and more established, best realistic migration target
- `WinUI/WPF`: true native, but basically a rebuild

My honest recommendation:

- if you want out of Electron, pick `Tauri` over `Electrobun` for this app

Because this app already has:

- custom titlebar logic
- main/preload bridge
- local cache/state
- embedded player/webview tricks

Tauri is the safer non-Electron path.

One important note:
Tauri uses the system webview, so Windows users depend on WebView2 being available; that’s part of the official setup story in Tauri docs. See [Prerequisites](https://v2.tauri.app/start/prerequisites/).

If you want, I can make a migration plan from this Electron app to Tauri, with:

1. what can stay
2. what must be rewritten
3. the risky parts, especially the player and ad-block/nav control logic

> we keeping elecctron

That’s a good call.

For this app, Electron is the least disruptive choice and it already fits the hard part: custom desktop shell plus messy embedded web player behavior. Moving to Tauri/Electrobun right now would mostly buy smaller packaging, but at the cost of a migration where the player and webview controls could get annoying fast.

So I’d treat the app as “shipping on Electron” and spend effort on polish:

- stability
- caching/perceived speed
- player behavior
- packaging/installer
- app icon, metadata, updates

The next meaningful step is probably turning it into a polished distributable Windows build rather than changing frameworks.

> I'm thinking of adding a book tab which contains mangas and books along with a small cbz etc reader that reads them later in the development

Yeah, that can fit the app well, but I’d treat it as a second product surface, not just “another tab.”

Because once `Books` exists, it pulls in a different shape of UX:

- different metadata
- different sources
- progress by page/chapter instead of runtime
- different artwork ratios
- eventually a real reader instead of a player

So I do think it’s a good idea, especially if you want `Velvet` to feel like an all-in-one media app. I’d just build it in phases:

1. `Books` tab first
   Show manga/books as discoverable cards, same visual language as the rest of the app.
2. Details modal adapted for books
   Author, chapters/volumes, status, genres, synopsis.
3. `Continue Reading`
   This is the book equivalent of Continue Watching, and honestly it’s the feature that makes the tab feel real.
4. Reader later
   Then add CBZ/CBR/PDF/EPUB support when we’re ready, instead of forcing it too early.

My recommendation:

- start with `Manga + Books` in one tab
- keep the first version browse-only
- design the data model now so `Continue Reading` and a future reader slot in cleanly later

The one thing worth deciding early is source strategy, because movies/TV are easy compared to books. Manga/books depend a lot more on where the metadata and files would come from, and that choice affects everything after it.

> where would be fetch the metadata of books from and also the content?

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> <details><summary>Searched web 6 times</summary>
>
> <details><summary>Searched web 6 times</summary>
>
> - Searched web for `Open Library API official documentation books metadata`
> - Searched web for `site:api.mangadex.org/docs MangaDex official docs`
> - Searched web for `MangaDex API official GitHub docs`
> - Searched web for `Google Books Embedded Viewer API official docs`
> - Searched web for `https://openlibrary.org/developers/api`
> - Searched web for `MangaDex rules official uploads official chapter links terms`
>
> </details>
>
> </details>

</details>

Yeah. The clean split is:

**Metadata**

- **Books:** [Open Library API](https://openlibrary.org/developers/api) for search, authors, editions, covers, and availability signals. Their [Search API](https://openlibrary.org/dev/docs/api/search) is especially good, and their [Books API](https://openlibrary.org/dev/docs/api/books?v=17) can resolve ISBN/OLID and preview links.
- **Books fallback/enrichment:** [Google Books API](https://developers.google.com/books/docs/overview) for richer descriptions, thumbnails, sale/release info, and preview/readability fields like `viewability`, `embeddable`, and `webReaderLink` in the [Volume resource](https://developers.google.com/books/docs/v1/reference/volumes).
- **Manga metadata:** [AniList GraphQL API](https://anilist.gitbook.io/anilist-apiv2-docs) is the nicest structured source for manga metadata.

**Content**

- **Best long-term path:** local imports first: `CBZ`, `CBR`, `EPUB`, `PDF`. That gives you a real reader without licensing mess.
- **Free/legal books online:** public-domain sources like [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/help/reading_options.html). For app integration, many people use Gutendex, but that’s not an official Gutenberg API.
- **Preview-only books:** [Google Books Embedded Viewer API](https://developers.google.com/books/docs/viewer/developers_guide) and Open Library/Internet Archive preview links when available.
- **Manga chapters/content:** this is the hard part. There isn’t a clean, mainstream, official “free full manga chapters API” for copyrighted content. If you want to stay on solid ground, I’d do:
  1. local `CBZ/CBR`
  2. metadata from AniList
  3. optional outbound links to official reading services
  4. avoid scraping/hosting random chapter sources

If we build this, my recommendation is:

- **Phase 1:** `Books` tab with metadata only
- **Phase 2:** local file import + `Continue Reading`
- **Phase 3:** actual reader
- **Phase 4:** optional online previews for books only

The short truth: **metadata is easy, content is where the legal and technical complexity starts**.

> we don't have to go legal way we're already watching movies otherwise since it is a personal project

Fair. For a personal project, the practical answer is different.

**Metadata**

- **Books:** `Open Library` first, `Google Books` as fallback/enrichment.
- **Manga:** `AniList` for clean metadata, sometimes `MangaDex` too if you want series/chapter structure.

**Content**

- **Manga:** easiest unofficial route is sources in the `MangaDex / manga aggregator` world, because chapters are image-based and easier to render in a reader.
- **Books:** much messier unofficially. There isn’t really one clean “movie-embed equivalent” for books. You usually end up with:
  - user-imported `epub/pdf/cbz`
  - or scraping/downloading from scattered sources
  - which is way more brittle than video embeds

So if the real goal is a future in-app reader, I’d recommend this split:

1. **Manga first**

- metadata from `AniList`
- chapter/content from a manga-oriented source
- reader built around image chapters
- this is the most realistic first win

2. **Books second**

- metadata from `Open Library` / `Google Books`
- actual reading content from imported `EPUB/PDF`
- much cleaner technically

That gives you:

- `Books` tab as a broad label
- inside it: `Manga` and `Books`
- but under the hood they work differently

My honest take: **manga is very doable, online book content is the messy part**. If we do this, I’d architect the tab now as two content types from day one instead of pretending they’re the same thing.

A strong stack would be:

- `Books tab`
- `Manga section`: AniList + manga chapter source
- `Books section`: Open Library/Google Books + local file imports later
- `Continue Reading` model shared across both

If you want, I can sketch the actual data model for `Books/Manga/Chapters/ReadingProgress` next.

What I was building toward is this: if we add a `Books` tab, we should model it as **one surface with two media types** underneath.

**Suggested structure**

- `Books` tab
- inside it:
  - `Manga`
  - `Books`

That lets the app feel unified, while the backend logic stays honest.

**Data model**

For both:

- `id`
- `type` = `book` or `manga`
- `title`
- `originalTitle`
- `cover`
- `description`
- `genres`
- `authors`
- `status`
- `year`
- `source`
- `externalUrl`

For manga:

- `chapters`
- `volumes`
- `chapterList`
- `readingMode` = `vertical` / `paged`
- `pages` per chapter later

For books:

- `pageCount`
- `format` = `epub` / `pdf` / `cbz` / `cbr`
- `filePath` later if imported
- `previewUrl` if online

**Progress model**

This is the important part if we want it to feel like the rest of the app.

Shared `Continue Reading` shape:

- `itemId`
- `type`
- `title`
- `cover`
- `progressType` = `chapter` or `page`
- `progress`
- `updatedAt`

For manga:

- current chapter
- current page inside that chapter

For books:

- current page
- maybe percentage too

So examples:

- manga: `Chapter 54, page 12`
- book: `Page 188 of 412`

**UI flow**

First version:

- add `Books` nav tab
- hero/banner optional, but probably better to keep it simpler than Movies
- rows like:
  - `Popular Manga`
  - `Trending Manga`
  - `Popular Books`
  - `Recently Added Files` later
  - `Continue Reading`

Modal:

- same system as current app
- but metadata changes:
  - manga: chapters, volumes, status
  - books: author, pages, year, format

**Reader plan**

For manga reader:

- vertical scroll reader first
- image pages
- next/previous chapter
- save progress on page/chapter change

For book reader:

- `PDF` first is easiest
- `EPUB` later
- `CBZ/CBR` can actually share some logic with manga because they’re page/image based

**Best implementation order**

1. `Books` tab shell
2. metadata fetch + rows
3. modal for books/manga
4. `Continue Reading`
5. manga reader
6. file import
7. PDF/EPUB reader later

**My recommendation**
If we do this, start with **manga-first** inside the Books tab. It maps better to the app’s current card/modal/player style, and a manga reader is much easier to build than a solid EPUB reader.

So the clean path is:

- `Books` tab
- first ship `Manga`
- then add `Books`
- then local reading support

Found and fixed the actual breaking bug.

The Manga tab wasn’t just “failing to load” generically — `mangaLatestPool()` in [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\api.js](./src/js/api.js) was requesting `limit=320` from MangaDex’s `/chapter` endpoint, and MangaDex rejects non-feed requests above `100`. So even after the `User-Agent` fix, the loader was still hard-failing before any manga could render.

I changed it to paginate properly in chunks of `100` and collect enough unique manga IDs across multiple pages instead of making one oversized request. I also already routed MangaDex through Electron with the required headers in:

- [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\main.js](./main.js)
- [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\preload.js](./preload.js)
- [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\api.js](./src/js/api.js)

> how does the reading system work

Right now it’s a built-in **manga chapter image reader**.

The flow is:

- `Manga` tab loads manga metadata from MangaDex
- clicking a card opens a manga-specific modal
- modal shows info + chapter list
- `Read Now` opens the local in-app reader overlay
- the reader fetches chapter page images and displays them in a vertical scroll stack

Technically, in [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\api.js](./src/js/api.js):

- `mangaChapterList(mangaId)` gets the readable English chapter list
- `mangaChapterPages(chapterId)` gets the page image URLs from MangaDex’s at-home server

Then in [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\app.js](./src/js/app.js):

- `openMangaModal(...)` loads details + chapters
- `openMangaReader(...)` opens the reader overlay
- `loadReaderChapter(...)` fetches the page URLs and renders each page as an `<img>`
- `saveReaderProgress()` stores progress in `localStorage` under `cinemax_manga_progress`

So the current reader is:

- vertical scrolling
- chapter based
- image page based
- local progress saved by current chapter + page index

It is **not** yet:

- EPUB/PDF/CBZ based
- a separate installed app
- a text reflow reader
- a two-page/paged comic reader

It’s basically a clean local shell around MangaDex chapter images.

> i need offline viewing capabilities for this project, since it is a personal practice project so adding it would be a good way to learn

Yes — and the best way to learn it in this project is to do it in **two very different tracks**:

1. **Manga offline**: very doable with the current architecture
2. **Movies/TV offline**: much harder, and with the current embed-based player, basically a different system

Given your codebase, I’d strongly recommend:

**Start with offline manga first.**

Why:

- you already have a local manga reader flow in [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\app.js](./src/js/app.js)
- manga content is just chapter image pages
- those can be downloaded, stored locally, and read later without the internet
- it teaches the right things: file storage, indexing, progress, cleanup, resumable downloads

For **movies/TV**, the current app uses third-party embeds, so “offline viewing” is not just a new feature. It would require a different backend path:

- actual downloadable files
- local media library
- probably a real video player instead of the current embed/webview flow

So the clean learning roadmap is:

**Phase 1: Offline manga**

- add `Download Chapter`
- save page images locally
- create a local chapter manifest JSON
- reader checks local files first, network second
- add `Downloaded` row / badge
- allow delete / clear storage

**Phase 2: Offline manga volumes**

- package chapter images as `cbz`
- optionally import local `cbz/cbr`

**Phase 3: Offline books**

- local `pdf/epub/cbz` imports

**Phase 4: Offline video**

- separate system, much bigger project

A good local storage shape would be something like:

- app data folder
- `downloads/manga/<mangaId>/<chapterId>/page-001.jpg`
- `downloads/manga/index.json`

And in app state:

- `downloaded`
- `downloadProgress`
- `localPath`
- `lastReadPage`

So the reader logic becomes:

- if chapter exists locally -> load local images
- else -> load remote MangaDex images

That would be a very solid feature and a genuinely good practice project.

My honest recommendation:

- **do not start with offline video**
- **build offline manga properly first**
- then expand to local book/comic formats

If you want, I can start implementing the **offline manga download system** directly in this codebase next.

I read [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\md\session_b_history.md](./md/session_b_history.md) and then audited the current downloads code against it.

Short version: the implementation was promising, but it was not fully correct yet. I found a few real issues and fixed the important ones.

What was wrong before:

- The download engine could detect direct `.mp4` streams, but the renderer still assumed everything was HLS and tried to parse them as manifests.
- HLS encryption metadata was parsed in [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\main.js](./main.js) but never actually used during assembly, which made encrypted streams shaky at best.
- Downloaded/downloading badges on row cards were mostly unwired because the cards rendered `data-key`, while the updater was looking for `data-item-id`.
- Offline playback from the Downloads page was still going through the embed webview path instead of a proper local `<video>` surface.
- The videos folder path was hardcoded from the home directory instead of using Electron’s videos path helper.

What I changed:

- In [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\main.js](./main.js), downloads now use `app.getPath("videos")` properly, stream resolution returns a stream type, manifest parsing keeps playlist metadata, and ffmpeg assembly now builds a local HLS playlist and uses saved key info when needed.
- In [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\app.js](./src/js/app.js), the renderer now handles both direct `.mp4` and HLS paths correctly, saves local key files for encrypted HLS, updates movie cards properly, updates episode download buttons more reliably, and shows a cleaner Downloads page state.
- In [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\index.html](./src/index.html) and [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\css\style.css](./src/css/style.css), I added a real local video element for offline playback instead of trying to treat the downloaded file like another remote embed.

I also fixed a smaller UI bug where failed or paused entries could leave the Downloads page looking oddly empty.

Validation:

- `node --check C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\main.js`
- `node --check C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\preload.js`
- `node --check C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\app.js`

One honest caveat: I haven’t live click-tested the whole Electron download flow in this turn, so I’d still treat this as “structurally corrected and much safer,” not “personally watched every edge case run in the window.” Also, direct `.mp4` downloads still won’t have the same restart-resume strength as segmented HLS downloads, because that resume model depends on segment files.

Since `main.js` changed, fully restart the app before testing downloads again.

U need to combine yt-dlp's built in resume feature with a persistent download state saved to disk.
> How it works
> yt-dlp already supports resuming via the --continue flag. It saves a .part file nd picks up from where it left off. U just need to persist the download metadata so after a restart u know wat was in progress.
>
> 1. Persist download state to JSON
>    jsconst fs = require('fs')
>    const path = require('path')
>
> const QUEUE_FILE = path.join(app.getPath('userData'), 'downloads.json')
>
> function saveQueue(queue) {
> fs.writeFileSync(QUEUE_FILE, JSON.stringify(queue, null, 2))
> }
>
> function loadQueue() {
> if (!fs.existsSync(QUEUE_FILE)) return []
> return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(QUEUE_FILE, 'utf-8'))
> }
> 2. Download entry structure
> js{
> id: 'uuid-or-tmdb-id',
> title: 'Inception',
> streamUrl: 'https://...',
> outputPath: 'C:/Users/.../Inception.mp4',
> status: 'paused', // pending | downloading | paused | done | failed
> progress: 47.3
> }
> 3. Resume aware download function
> jsfunction downloadWithResume(entry, onProgress) {
> return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
> const args = [
> entry.streamUrl,
> '--ffmpeg-location', ffmpegPath,
> '-o', entry.outputPath,
> '--continue',      // resume .part file
> '--newline'
> ]
>
> const proc = execFile(ytdlpPath, args)
> entry.status = 'downloading'
> saveQueue(loadQueue().map(q => q.id === entry.id ? entry : q))
>
> proc.stdout.on('data', (data) => {
> const match = data.match(/(\d+\.?\d*)%/)
> if (match) {
> entry.progress = parseFloat(match[1])
> entry.status = 'downloading'
> saveQueue(loadQueue().map(q => q.id === entry.id ? entry : q))
> onProgress(entry.id, entry.progress)
> }
> })
>
> proc.on('close', (code) => {
> entry.status = code === 0 ? 'done' : 'failed'
> saveQueue(loadQueue().map(q => q.id === entry.id ? entry : q))
> code === 0 ? resolve() : reject()
> })
> })
> }
> 4. On app startup, auto resume
> jsapp.whenReady().then(() => {
> const queue = loadQueue()
> const incomplete = queue.filter(q =>
> q.status === 'downloading' || q.status === 'pending'
> )
>
> for (const entry of incomplete) {
> entry.status = 'pending'
> downloadWithResume(entry, (id, progress) => {
> mainWindow.webContents.send('download-progress', { id, progress })
> })
> }
> })
> 5. Handle the .part file
> yt-dlp saves progress as Inception.mp4.part. The --continue flag tells it to detect this file nd resume from its byte offset. U don't need to manage this manually, yt-dlp handles it. Just make sure u never delete .part files until download is done.
> One edge case
> Stream URLs from VidSrc expire after a while, so if the PC was off for a long time the saved streamUrl might be stale. Handle this by re-fetching the stream URL on resume:
> jsasync function resumeEntry(entry) {
> try {
> // re-fetch fresh stream url before resuming
> entry.streamUrl = await getStreamUrl(entry.embedUrl)
> saveQueue(loadQueue().map(q => q.id === entry.id ? entry : q))
> await downloadWithResume(entry, ...)
> } catch {
> entry.status = 'failed'
> saveQueue(...)
> }
> }
> So store both embedUrl (permanent) nd streamUrl (temporary) in each entry. Always re-extract streamUrl on resume.

Yeah, for this app I think `yt-dlp` is the better direction.

Based on your current logs, the weak point is still stream discovery:

- the embed page loads
- network activity happens
- but your custom resolver never sees a usable `.m3u8` or `.mp4`

That is exactly the kind of brittle extraction problem `yt-dlp` is better at than our hand-rolled CDP path.

My take:

- `Yes`: switch the download backend to `yt-dlp + ffmpeg`
- `No`: don’t throw away your UI, queue, manifest, and downloads page
- `Also no`: I wouldn’t blindly copy Claude’s exact code shape

What I’d keep from your current system:

- Downloads page
- manifest/state files
- episode-level buttons
- local playback in the app
- your own folder structure under `Videos\Velvet`

What I’d replace:

- `download-resolve-stream`
- custom manifest parsing
- custom segment downloading
- custom HLS assembly path

Why I’d switch:

1. `yt-dlp` already handles a lot of extractor breakage better than our custom resolver.
2. Resume is already a first-class feature there: `-c/--continue` and `.part` files are documented.
3. It can expose URLs with `-g/--get-url`, but more importantly, it can often download directly without us micromanaging manifests.
4. The docs explicitly recommend using structured output like `--progress-template` instead of scraping generic stdout, which is cleaner than the current progress parsing idea.
   Sources: [yt-dlp README](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp), [`--continue`](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/blob/master/README.md), [`--get-url`](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/blob/master/README.md), [`--progress-template`](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/blob/master/README.md)

What I would change from Claude’s suggestion:

- I would **not** use `--get-url` as the main path unless needed. Better to let `yt-dlp` do extraction + download in one flow when possible.
- I would **not** parse normal stdout with a regex if I can avoid it. The README says normal stdout is not the stable interface; `--progress-template` is the better path.
- I would probably call the binary directly with `child_process.spawn`, not rely on `yt-dlp-wrap` unless it buys something real.
- I would store:
  - `embedUrl`
  - `outputPath`
  - `status`
  - `progress`
  - maybe last-known extractor info
  - but not depend on a saved direct stream URL surviving restart

One important caution:

- `yt-dlp` is not magic. If VidSrc changes or blocks extraction, it can still fail.
- But it’s a much stronger foundation than the current custom resolver.

So my recommendation is:

**Best path**

1. Keep the current UI/state layer
2. Replace the backend download engine with `yt-dlp`
3. Use `ffmpeg` through `yt-dlp`
4. Use `--continue`
5. Use `--progress-template` for progress events
6. Keep your timestamped log file

Given where your logs are pointing, I think continuing to patch the custom resolver is the worse bet.

I can do the migration carefully:

- first add `yt-dlp` as an alternate backend behind one code path
- test movie + single TV episode
- then remove the custom segment engine once the new path proves itself

Sources:

- [yt-dlp README](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp)
- [yt-dlp update channels; nightly recommended for regular users](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp)
- [Embedding guidance; prefer structured output like `--progress-template`](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/blob/master/README.md)

I kept going and did a real cleanup pass on the downloads feature.

The important part is that the implementation now makes more sense as a hybrid:

- keep our own stream resolver for VidSrc discovery
- let `yt-dlp + ffmpeg` do the actual transfer, resume, and assembly

I tightened that in [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\main.js](./main.js) and [C:\Users\Abdullah\Desktop\app\src\js\app.js](./src/js/app.js).

What I fixed:

- paused/failed downloads can now `Resume` / `Retry` from the Downloads page instead of just sitting there
- renderer now listens for `complete`, `cancelled`, and `error` download events too, not just progress
- cancelled/resume-failed jobs now update manifest state properly instead of getting stuck in a vague state
- deleting a download now also removes yt-dlp sidecar files like `.part` and `.ytdl`
- job registration now tracks the spawned yt-dlp process cleanly for cancellation
- yt-dlp runs with `--no-playlist` now, which is safer for direct media URLs
- the resolver got a stronger nudge path: real input events plus autoplay allowance, not just JS click simulation

I also verified the backend toolchain itself:

- `yt-dlp` found at `C:\ytdlp\yt-dlp.exe`
- `ffmpeg` found at `C:\ytdlp\ffmpeg.exe`

And I did a live transfer smoke test against a public HLS stream. It successfully started downloading and wrote real partial files before I killed it and cleaned everything up. So the `yt-dlp + ffmpeg` side is alive; the remaining fragile bit is still VidSrc stream discovery.

That means the honest state is:

- the download backend is in much better shape now
- the last real risk is still whether a given VidSrc page exposes a stream reliably enough for the resolver to catch it
